The book of ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧ closed with a nation at rest. The tribes had their land, the old leader had made them promise at ⟦l:shechem_1069|Shechem⟧ to serve the Lord alone, and Joshua, ⟦p:joseph_1710|Joseph⟧'s bones and ⟦p:eleazar_1062|Eleazar⟧ the priest were laid in their graves. The book of Judges opens in the generation that follows, and it tells what became of that promise.

The answer is not a happy one. Judges covers the long stretch of time between the settlement of ⟦p:canaan_914|Canaan⟧ and the rise of Israel's first king. Israel in these years is not a kingdom but a loose federation of tribes, each living on its own allotted land, with no capital, no standing army and no central government. The tabernacle stands at ⟦l:shiloh_1081|Shiloh⟧ in the hill country of ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧, but most of the time the tribes act alone, and sometimes against each other.

They also share the land with others. ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧ warned that the Canaanites who remained would become a snare, and Judges opens by listing, tribe by tribe, the towns they failed to take. Canaanite cities still hold the fertile valleys and the coast, with their iron chariots and their gods: ⟦p:baal_573|Baal⟧, the storm god who was believed to bring the rains and the harvest, and the goddesses Asherah and Ashtoreth. Around the edges of Israel's territory press other peoples, Moabites and ⟦l:ammon_58|Ammonites⟧ from across the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧, Midianite raiders from the desert, and, increasingly, the Philistines, who had settled on the southern coastal plain and would become Israel's most dangerous enemy.

The book takes its name from the leaders God raises up in these years. The Hebrew word usually translated judges means something broader than a magistrate. A few of them settle disputes, but most are deliverers, local champions who rally one tribe or a handful of tribes to throw off an oppressor. They are an unlikely company: ⟦p:ehud_1039|Ehud⟧, a left-handed man from the small tribe of ⟦p:benjamin_463|Benjamin⟧; ⟦p:deborah_997|Deborah⟧, a prophetess who judges Israel beneath a palm tree; ⟦p:gideon_1314|Gideon⟧, the youngest son of an unimportant family, threshing wheat in hiding; ⟦p:jephthah_839|Jephthah⟧, the son of a prostitute, driven out by his brothers; and ⟦p:samson_2468|Samson⟧, a man of enormous strength and very little self-control. Alongside these are several minor judges, mentioned in a sentence or two.

The stories follow a pattern that the second chapter spells out in advance. Israel does evil in the sight of the Lord and serves other gods. The Lord hands them over to an oppressor. In their distress they cry out, and the Lord raises up a deliverer, who rescues them. The land has rest, often for forty years. Then the deliverer dies, and the cycle begins again. But the cycle is not a circle. It is a downward spiral. ⟦p:othniel_2259|Othniel⟧, the first judge, is a model leader. By the time of ⟦p:gideon_1314|Gideon⟧, the deliverer himself makes an object that leads Israel astray, and his son ⟦p:abimelech_41|Abimelech⟧ murders his brothers to make himself king. ⟦p:jephthah_839|Jephthah⟧'s rash vow ends in grief. ⟦p:samson_2468|Samson⟧, the last of the great judges, fights the Philistines alone, again and again to settle a personal score, and he never brings the land rest.

The final chapters drop the pattern altogether. There are no more deliverers, only two disturbing stories from the life of the tribes. One concerns a household shrine, a wandering Levite and the migration of the tribe of ⟦p:dan_973|Dan⟧. The other concerns a crime at ⟦l:gibeah_466|Gibeah⟧ in ⟦p:benjamin_463|Benjamin⟧ so terrible that it leads to civil war. Through these chapters runs a refrain: in those days there was no king in Israel, and everyone did what was right in his own eyes.

That refrain looks back on these years from a time when Israel did have a king. The author is not named. Jewish tradition credits ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧, and the book belongs with the histories that follow it. Most of the judges are local figures, leading their own tribes in their own corner of the land.

Judges is one of the most honest books in the Bible about the failures of God's people, and it does not soften them. Yet through all of it God keeps answering their cries and raising up rescuers, however flawed. The gentle story of ⟦p:ruth_2450|Ruth⟧ is set in these same years, and the book of First ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ will carry the history on, through the last of the judges, toward the question the refrain keeps raising: what kind of king Israel needs.
1:
⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧ is dead, and Israel has no single leader to take his place. The tribes have their allotted land, but much of it is still held by Canaanites, and the book begins with the people asking the Lord which tribe should go up first to fight. The answer is ⟦l:judah_1280|Judah⟧.

The chapter is a survey of the tribes' efforts to take possession of their territory, moving roughly from south to north. Some of it repeats material from the book of ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧, such as ⟦p:caleb_537|Caleb⟧'s offer of his daughter Acsah to whoever captures ⟦l:debir_325|Debir⟧, and ⟦p:othniel_2259|Othniel⟧'s success there. The book is gathering the threads of the settlement together rather than telling events in strict order. ⟦l:judah_1280|Judah⟧ begins well, with victories in the hill country and the south, though its troops cannot overcome the iron chariots of the plains.

As the survey moves north, the tone changes. ⟦l:benjamin-territory_1293|Benjamin⟧ does not drive the ⟦p:jebusite_748|Jebusites⟧ out of ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧. Then comes a list of tribes that fail, ⟦p:manasseh_1928|Manasseh⟧, ⟦l:ephraim-territory_1292|Ephraim⟧, ⟦p:zebulun_3002|Zebulun⟧, ⟦p:asher_337|Asher⟧, ⟦p:naphtali_2149|Naphtali⟧, and finally ⟦p:dan_973|Dan⟧, which is pushed back into the hills by the ⟦p:amorite_237|Amorites⟧. The phrase did not drive out becomes a drumbeat. The land is shared, not taken.
2:
The previous chapter recorded the tribes' failure to drive out the Canaanites. Now the angel of the Lord comes up from ⟦l:gilgal_476|Gilgal⟧, Israel's first camp in the land, to a place called ⟦l:bochim_252|Bochim⟧, and he gives God's verdict. Israel has made agreements with the peoples of the land and has not torn down their altars. So the Lord will no longer drive those peoples out; they will be thorns in Israel's side. The people weep, and the place is named Bochim, which means weepers.

The chapter then steps back and restates the death of ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧, as if beginning again. While Joshua and the elders who outlived him were alive, the people served the Lord. But a new generation grows up who do not know the Lord or what he has done.

The rest of the chapter is unusual: it summarises the whole book before the stories begin. It describes the cycle that will repeat again and again: Israel turns to the Baals, God gives them over to their enemies, they groan under oppression, God raises up a judge to save them, and after the judge's death they fall back further than before. The listener is given the key to everything that follows.
3:
The pattern has been laid out, and now it begins. The chapter opens by naming the nations left in the land to test Israel, the Philistines, Canaanites, Sidonians and ⟦p:hivite_1534|Hivites⟧, and it records the first step of compromise: Israelites marrying into these peoples and serving their gods.

Then come the first three deliverers. ⟦p:othniel_2259|Othniel⟧, ⟦p:caleb_537|Caleb⟧'s nephew, whom we met capturing Debir, rescues Israel from a king named Cushan-rishathaim of ⟦l:mesopotamia_790|Aram-naharaim⟧, the land of the two rivers in northern ⟦l:mesopotamia_790|Mesopotamia⟧. His story is told in a few lines and contains every element of the pattern, like a template for what follows.

The second story is very different, full of vivid and earthy detail. ⟦p:eglon_1037|Eglon⟧, king of ⟦l:moab_815|Moab⟧, has crossed the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧ with his allies and occupied ⟦l:jericho_634|Jericho⟧, the City of Palms, and for eighteen years Israel pays him tribute. The deliverer is ⟦p:ehud_1039|Ehud⟧, from the tribe of ⟦p:benjamin_463|Benjamin⟧, and his left-handedness will matter. The chapter ends with a single sentence about a third figure, ⟦p:shamgar_2534|Shamgar⟧ son of ⟦p:anath_261|Anath⟧, who strikes down six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad, the long pointed stick used for driving cattle.
4:
After ⟦p:ehud_1039|Ehud⟧'s death, Israel again does evil, and this time the oppressor is a Canaanite king, ⟦p:jabin_677|Jabin⟧ of ⟦l:hazor_545|Hazor⟧ in the far north. A king of Hazor with the same name was defeated in ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧'s day, and now Hazor is strong again. Its army commander is ⟦p:sisera_2757|Sisera⟧, and its strength is nine hundred iron chariots. For twenty years Jabin harshly oppresses Israel.

The judge in these days is ⟦p:deborah_997|Deborah⟧, a prophetess, who sits under a palm tree in the hill country of ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧, between ⟦l:ramah_972|Ramah⟧ and ⟦l:bethel_202|Bethel⟧, where the Israelites come to her for judgement. She summons a man named ⟦p:barak_401|Barak⟧ from ⟦l:kedesh_676|Kedesh⟧ in ⟦p:naphtali_2149|Naphtali⟧ and passes on God's command: gather ten thousand men from Naphtali and ⟦p:zebulun_3002|Zebulun⟧ on ⟦l:mount_tabor_857|Mount Tabor⟧, a rounded hill that rises above the Jezreel Valley. Barak's hesitation, and Deborah's answer to it, set up a twist at the end of the story.

The battle takes place by the River ⟦l:kishon_705|Kishon⟧, which flows through the valley toward the sea. Notice too a minor character introduced in passing: ⟦p:heber_1470|Heber⟧ the Kenite, distantly related to ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧' father-in-law, who has pitched his tent near ⟦l:kedesh_676|Kedesh⟧. His wife's name is ⟦p:jael_689|Jael⟧.
5:
The battle by the ⟦l:kishon_705|Kishon⟧ is over. ⟦p:sisera_2757|Sisera⟧ is dead at the hand of ⟦p:jael_689|Jael⟧, and Jabin's grip on the north is broken. Now ⟦p:deborah_997|Deborah⟧ and ⟦p:barak_401|Barak⟧ sing.

Their song tells the same story as the chapter before, but in a very different way. Where chapter four was prose and narrative, chapter five is celebration, full of sound and movement. Early in the song the Lord marches out from ⟦l:seir_1042|Seir⟧, in the south, the One of ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧, and the earth trembles before him.

The song also fills in details the prose left out. It describes how dangerous life had become under the Canaanites, with roads deserted and village life at a standstill. It calls the roll of the tribes, praising those who came to fight and rebuking those who stayed at home, among them ⟦p:reuben_2429|Reuben⟧, ⟦p:dan_973|Dan⟧ and ⟦p:asher_337|Asher⟧. It hints that a storm turned the battle, with the stars fighting from heaven and the river sweeping the enemy away.

At its close the song turns to two women. One is ⟦p:jael_689|Jael⟧, celebrated in vivid verse. The other is ⟦p:sisera_2757|Sisera⟧'s mother, looking out through her lattice window, waiting for a son who will never come home.
6:
The land has had forty years of rest since the song of ⟦p:deborah_997|Deborah⟧. Then Israel again does evil, and this time the oppression comes from the desert. The Midianites, with the Amalekites and other peoples of the east, sweep in whenever Israel's crops are sown, like a swarm of locusts, with their tents, flocks and camels, and strip the land as far as ⟦l:gaza_446|Gaza⟧ on the coast. The Israelites retreat to caves and mountain strongholds.

When the people cry out, God first sends a prophet to remind them why this is happening. Then the angel of the Lord appears at ⟦l:ophrah_914|Ophrah⟧, in the territory of ⟦p:manasseh_1928|Manasseh⟧, under an oak belonging to a man named ⟦p:joash_1630|Joash⟧. His son ⟦p:gideon_1314|Gideon⟧ is threshing wheat, not on an open threshing floor where the wind would carry away the chaff, but down in a winepress, out of sight of the raiders.

The angel greets him as a mighty man of valour. What follows is a call, a sign, and a dangerous first assignment close to home, because ⟦p:gideon_1314|Gideon⟧'s own father keeps an altar to ⟦p:baal_573|Baal⟧. By the end of the chapter the Midianite armies have crossed the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧ and camped in the ⟦l:valley_of_jezreel_1211|Valley of Jezreel⟧, and Gideon, still uncertain, asks God for signs with a fleece of wool.
7:
⟦p:gideon_1314|Gideon⟧ has his answer from the fleece, and he and his men camp by the spring of ⟦l:harod_529|Harod⟧, on the slopes above the ⟦l:valley_of_jezreel_1211|Valley of Jezreel⟧. Below them, near the hill of Moreh, lies the vast camp of ⟦l:midian_796|Midian⟧.

⟦p:gideon_1314|Gideon⟧ has gathered more than thirty thousand men from ⟦p:manasseh_1928|Manasseh⟧ and the northern tribes. Against a host as numerous as locusts, it is hardly a large army. God's view is the opposite: there are too many, and if Israel wins with an army this size, they will think they saved themselves. So the army is reduced, first by sending home everyone who is afraid, and then by a strange test at the water's edge, until only three hundred remain.

Then, by night, God tells ⟦p:gideon_1314|Gideon⟧ to go down to the enemy camp, and gently adds that if he is afraid he may take his servant Purah with him. What Gideon overhears among the Midianite tents gives him the courage he needs. The attack that follows uses rams' horns, clay jars and torches rather than swords, and by the end of the chapter the men of ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧ have joined the pursuit, seized the waters of the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧ and captured two Midianite princes.
8:
The Midianite army has broken and fled, but the fighting is not over. The chapter opens with a quarrel. The proud tribe of ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧, which has just captured the Midianite princes ⟦p:oreb_2255|Oreb⟧ and ⟦p:zeeb_3033|Zeeb⟧, is angry that ⟦p:gideon_1314|Gideon⟧ did not call them sooner, and Gideon calms them with a gracious answer.

Then he crosses the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧ in pursuit of the two kings of ⟦l:midian_796|Midian⟧, ⟦p:zebah_2997|Zebah⟧ and ⟦p:zalmunna_2983|Zalmunna⟧, with his three hundred exhausted men. On the eastern side, the Israelite towns of ⟦l:succoth_1113|Succoth⟧ and ⟦l:penuel_931|Penuel⟧ refuse to feed his troops, unwilling to risk Midian's revenge before the war is won. ⟦p:gideon_1314|Gideon⟧ warns them that he will be back.

The second half of the chapter shows a harder, more complicated man than the hesitant farmer of chapter six. ⟦p:gideon_1314|Gideon⟧ has scores to settle, and the reason for his pursuit of the two kings turns out to be personal. When the people offer him and his descendants the right to rule over them, his answer sounds exactly right. But what he does next with the gold of ⟦l:midian_796|Midian⟧ casts a long shadow. The chapter ends with Gideon's death, a note about a son named ⟦p:abimelech_41|Abimelech⟧, born to a concubine in ⟦l:shechem_1069|Shechem⟧, and Israel's swift return to ⟦p:baal_573|Baal⟧.
9:
⟦p:gideon_1314|Gideon⟧ refused to be king, but one of his sons has no such hesitation. ⟦p:abimelech_41|Abimelech⟧, the son of Gideon's concubine in ⟦l:shechem_1069|Shechem⟧, goes to his mother's relatives there and makes them an offer: would they rather be ruled by the seventy sons of Gideon, also called ⟦p:gideon_1314|Jerubbaal⟧, or by one man who is their own flesh and blood?

⟦l:shechem_1069|Shechem⟧ is an old Canaanite city in the hill country of ⟦p:manasseh_1928|Manasseh⟧ and ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧, the same place where ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧ renewed the covenant. Its leaders fund ⟦p:abimelech_41|Abimelech⟧ from the temple of Baal-berith, and with that money he hires a band of reckless men. What he does at his father's house in ⟦l:ophrah_914|Ophrah⟧ leaves only one brother alive, the youngest, ⟦p:jotham_1734|Jotham⟧.

From the slopes of ⟦l:mount_gerizim_836|Mount Gerizim⟧, above ⟦l:shechem_1069|Shechem⟧, ⟦p:jotham_1734|Jotham⟧ shouts a parable to the city, the first fable in the Bible, about trees looking for a king. It ends with a curse. The rest of the chapter traces how that curse works itself out over the three years of ⟦p:abimelech_41|Abimelech⟧'s rule, through suspicion, rebellion and burning towers. This is the first attempt at kingship in Israel, and it is a dark one.
10:
⟦p:abimelech_41|Abimelech⟧ is dead, killed by a millstone dropped from a tower, and his short and violent reign is over. The chapter begins quietly, with two lesser judges remembered in a few lines each. ⟦p:tola_2879|Tola⟧, from the tribe of ⟦p:issachar_645|Issachar⟧, judges Israel for twenty-three years from ⟦l:shamir_1061|Shamir⟧ in the hill country of ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧. ⟦p:jair_709|Jair⟧, from ⟦l:gilead_475|Gilead⟧ east of the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧, judges for twenty-two, and his thirty sons on thirty donkeys suggest wealth and status.

Then the cycle turns again, and more darkly than before. The list of foreign gods Israel now serves is longer than ever: the Baals and Ashtoreths, and the gods of ⟦l:syria_1122|Aram⟧, ⟦l:sidon_1093|Sidon⟧, ⟦l:moab_815|Moab⟧, ⟦l:ammon_58|Ammon⟧ and the Philistines. Two oppressors rise at once, the Philistines in the west and the ⟦l:ammon_58|Ammonites⟧ in the east. The chapter concentrates on the Ammonites, who press hard on the Israelites in ⟦l:gilead_475|Gilead⟧ for eighteen years and even cross the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧ to raid ⟦l:judah_1280|Judah⟧, ⟦p:benjamin_463|Benjamin⟧ and ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧.

When Israel cries out this time, God's reply is unexpectedly sharp, and the people's answer is more than words. The chapter ends with the armies of ⟦l:ammon_58|Ammon⟧ and Israel facing each other in ⟦l:gilead_475|Gilead⟧, and the leaders of Gilead searching for someone, anyone, willing to lead the attack.
11:
The ⟦l:ammon_58|Ammonites⟧ are camped in ⟦l:gilead_475|Gilead⟧, and the Gileadites at ⟦l:mizpah_809|Mizpah⟧, without a commander. The man they turn to is ⟦p:jephthah_839|Jephthah⟧, a mighty warrior with a troubled past. He is the son of a man named Gilead and a prostitute, and his half-brothers drove him out to keep him from any share of the inheritance. He has since lived in the land of Tob, to the north-east, at the head of a band of outlaws.

Now the elders who rejected him come asking for help, and ⟦p:jephthah_839|Jephthah⟧ drives a hard bargain. If he fights, he will be their head.

Before going to war, ⟦p:jephthah_839|Jephthah⟧ tries diplomacy. His message to the king of ⟦l:ammon_58|Ammon⟧ is a careful history lesson, recalling Israel's journey from ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, the refusal of ⟦l:edom_357|Edom⟧ and ⟦l:moab_815|Moab⟧ to let them pass, and the defeat of the ⟦p:amorite_237|Amorite⟧ king ⟦p:sihon_2739|Sihon⟧, whose land Israel took. He claims Israel has held that land for three hundred years.

Then ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|the Spirit⟧ of the Lord comes on ⟦p:jephthah_839|Jephthah⟧, and he marches. But before the battle he makes a vow, and its consequences turn his victory into one of the saddest scenes in the Old Testament. The text tells what follows in spare and restrained words.
12:
⟦p:jephthah_839|Jephthah⟧ has defeated the ⟦l:ammon_58|Ammonites⟧, but there is no peace. Once again the tribe of ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧ feels slighted. They complained to ⟦p:gideon_1314|Gideon⟧ for not calling them sooner, and Gideon calmed them with a soft answer. Now they cross the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧ to confront Jephthah with the same complaint, and with a threat to burn his house down around him.

⟦p:jephthah_839|Jephthah⟧ is not ⟦p:gideon_1314|Gideon⟧, and this time the quarrel turns into war between Israelite tribes. The fighting ends at the fords of the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧ with a test of pronunciation. Ephraimites spoke with a different accent from the men of ⟦l:gilead_475|Gilead⟧, and a single word, shibboleth, gives them away. The word has passed into the English language as a test that marks out who belongs.

⟦p:jephthah_839|Jephthah⟧ judges Israel for six years. The chapter then records three more minor judges in quick succession: ⟦p:ibzan_1588|Ibzan⟧ of ⟦l:bethlehem_218|Bethlehem⟧, ⟦p:elon_1184|Elon⟧ of ⟦p:zebulun_3002|Zebulun⟧, and ⟦p:abdon_10|Abdon⟧ of ⟦l:pirathon_949|Pirathon⟧ in ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧. Their large families, arranged marriages and many donkeys suggest leaders of local prominence and wealth. None of them leads Israel into battle, and none is said to have saved anyone.
13:
After the minor judges, the familiar opening returns: the Israelites again do evil, and the Lord gives them into the hands of the Philistines for forty years. This is the longest oppression in the book, and for the first time there is no mention of Israel crying out for help.

The Philistines were a seafaring people who had settled on the southern coastal plain, in five cities ruled by five lords, and they were pushing inland into the ⟦l:shephelah_1074|foothills⟧ where the tribe of ⟦p:dan_973|Dan⟧ was trying to settle.

The story begins in the Danite town of ⟦l:zorah_1275|Zorah⟧, in the ⟦l:shephelah_1074|foothills⟧ west of ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, with a couple who have no children. Like ⟦p:sarah_2473|Sarah⟧, ⟦p:rebekah_2401|Rebekah⟧ and ⟦p:rachel_2386|Rachel⟧ before her, ⟦p:manoah_1933|Manoah⟧'s wife is barren, and like them she receives a promise. The angel of the Lord tells her she will have a son, who must be a Nazirite from birth. In the law of ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧, a Nazirite was someone set apart to God by a special vow: no wine or grapes, no contact with the dead, and no razor on the head. This child will be set apart for life, and he will begin to rescue Israel from the Philistines.

⟦p:manoah_1933|Manoah⟧'s eager questions and his wife's calm good sense make this one of the gentlest scenes in Judges. The child's name is ⟦p:samson_2468|Samson⟧.
14:
⟦p:samson_2468|Samson⟧ has grown up in ⟦l:zorah_1275|Zorah⟧, and ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|the Spirit⟧ of the Lord has begun to stir him. Now he goes down from the hills to ⟦l:timnah_1164|Timnah⟧, a town in the valley below, on the border with Philistine territory, and sees a young Philistine woman he wants to marry.

His parents object. Israel had been warned against marrying into the peoples of the land, and the Philistines, uncircumcised and ruling over Israel, were the last family they would choose. But ⟦p:samson_2468|Samson⟧ insists, because she is pleasing in his eyes, a phrase worth remembering in a book that ends with everyone doing what is right in his own eyes. The narrator adds that, unknown to them, the Lord is using this to bring about a confrontation with the Philistines.

What follows is the first of ⟦p:samson_2468|Samson⟧'s adventures, and it introduces his character: enormous physical strength, given by ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|the Spirit⟧ of the Lord, and a talent for riddles and wordplay, joined to impulsiveness, secrecy and a quick temper. A lion in the vineyards, a wedding feast, a riddle and a wager lead, by the seventh day of the celebration, to violence and a broken marriage.
15:
